title: How await works: continuations, contexts and pitfalls
body: The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine. At each `await`, if the task has already completed the method simply continues synchronously; otherwise it registers the rest of the method as a continuation and returns. When the task completes, the continuation runs, possibly on a different thread.

Where the continuation runs depends on the captured context. In UI frameworks a `SynchronizationContext` brings it back to the UI thread; in ASP.NET Core and console apps there is no such context, so it runs on a thread-pool thread. Library code that does not need the original context can use `await task.ConfigureAwait(false)` to avoid the cost and avoid deadlocks when a caller blocks.

Blocking on async code (`task.Result`, `task.Wait()`, `GetAwaiter().GetResult()`) is called sync-over-async. On a single-threaded context it can deadlock: the blocked thread waits for a continuation that needs that same thread. Elsewhere it wastes a thread and can starve the pool. Make the call chain async all the way up instead.

`async void` methods cannot be awaited and their exceptions are raised on the captured context, typically crashing the process. Use them only for event handlers. An exception in an `async Task` method is stored in the task and rethrown at `await`, which is where you catch it.

Code before the first incomplete `await` runs synchronously on the caller's thread, including argument validation. Check that expensive synchronous work is not hiding before the first await, and that `.Result`/`.Wait()` never appear in code that could run on a context-bound thread.

challenge: Write an async method ValidateAndDelayAsync(int ms) that must throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException immediately (at the call, not at await) for negative input. Use a non-async wrapper with a local async function and show the exception is thrown before any await.
solutionStdout:
thrown at the call site
valid call completed
question: Why is calling `.Result` on a task from a UI thread risky?
correct: The continuation may need the blocked UI thread, causing a deadlock
wrong: Result always returns null for incomplete tasks
reasoning: Sync-over-async blocks the thread the async continuation is waiting to run on; go async all the way.
